# Homework 09 — Pivoting a Different Great Lake

### How to turn it in

**Quarto** homework — fill in this `.qmd`, **Render**, and submit both files.

::: callout-tip
## Loading the data — straight from NOAA (a URL!)

The ice files already live on the web, so no local copy is needed — just change
the lake code in the link. Pick one: `mic.txt` (Michigan), `hur.txt` (Huron),
`eri.txt` (Erie), or `ont.txt` (Ontario).

``` r
library(tidyverse)
url <- "https://www.glerl.noaa.gov/data/ice/glicd/daily/eri.txt"   # <- your lake
ice_raw <- read.table(url, header = TRUE, na.strings = c("-999", "-99.00", "NA")) %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "date") %>%
  as_tibble()
```
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Task 1 — Read + inspect (2 pts)

Load your chosen lake and run `dim()`. How many year-columns are there?

### Task 2 — Pivot to long (2 pts)

Use `pivot_longer()` to collapse the year-columns into a `year` column (strip the `"X"` prefix) and an `ice_cover` column. Show the first rows.

### Task 3 — Yearly maximum (2 pts)

Fix the year to numeric, drop missing ice values, then for each `year` keep the single highest ice-cover row with `slice_max()`.

### Task 4 — The twist: compare to Superior (2 pts)

Fit `lm(ice_cover ~ year)` on your lake's yearly maxima and report the slope (per year). Lake Superior's max-ice slope is roughly **−0.3 %/year**. Is your lake losing ice faster or slower?

### Task 5 — Explain (2 pts)

In 1–2 sentences: your lake is shallower/deeper than Superior — how might that affect how fast its ice responds to warming?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

10 pts: T1 read + count (2) · T2 correct pivot_longer w/ names_prefix (2) · T3 date fix + slice_max (2) · T4 lm slope + comparison to Superior (2) · T5 reasonable physical reasoning (2). Struggle point: adapting the whole workflow to a new file and interpreting a slope comparison.
